anchors.title: Should schools teach financial literacy as a required course?
anchors.body:
I graduated high school without ever learning how to do my taxes, understand a mortgage, or create a budget. Meanwhile, I took two years of a language I've never used since.

Should personal finance be a required course in Oregon high schools? What would you cut to make room for it, or should the school year be extended?

comments.body: Absolutely yes. The number of young adults who don't understand compound interest or how credit scores work is staggering. This is a life skill, not an elective.

replies.body: The challenge is finding qualified teachers. Most high school teachers don't have personal finance backgrounds. We'd need serious professional development.

comments.body: I'd argue financial literacy should replace part of the existing math curriculum in junior and senior year. Most students don't need calculus, but everyone needs to understand budgeting.

replies.body: Disagree on replacing math. Calculus and statistics are foundational for STEM careers. Add financial literacy without gutting the math program.

anchors.title: Proposal: Mandate financial literacy in Oregon high schools
anchors.body:
Building on the community discussion, I'd like to propose that Oregon require all public high school students to complete a one-semester personal finance course before graduation.

The course would cover: budgeting, taxes, credit and debt, investing basics, insurance, and renting vs. buying. It could be offered as a standalone course or integrated into existing social studies requirements.

Funding could come from the Student Success Act allocation for career-technical education. What do you think?

comments.body: I support this in principle, but the implementation details matter a lot. Who writes the curriculum? The financial industry has a history of pushing self-serving 'literacy' programs.

replies.body: Great point. The curriculum should be developed by educators and consumer advocates, not banks or credit card companies.

comments.body: One semester isn't enough. Financial literacy should be woven through multiple years, starting in middle school with basic concepts and building to more complex topics.
